Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: 02 - C++ - Objects, Ownership and Lifetime - Visual Recall — C++: Objects, Ownership and Lifetime — Visual Recall Scope: Companion to Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs. A compact teaching board, not a substitute for the worked chapter. Draw each model from memory; explain every arrow and state its preconditions. One-page short notes Story stop Shortest useful note Open the explanation / figure Build Translation makes declarations visible, definitions executable, and linking joins program pieces. Build pipeline · Modules Object Storage is the place; lifetime is the interval; identity is the occupant. Same address does not promise same object. Storage/object figure · Generation handle Borrow A pointer/reference/view grants access, not ownership. Validity depends on the referent, lifetime, mutation, and invalidation contract. Borrow hazards · Deferred views Value Construction creates; assignment replaces; move may transfer responsibility while source remains alive. Rule of Zero composes tested owners. Construction/destruction · Rule of Zero Resource RAII binds cleanup to an owner lifetime; external users may require deferred release. Four-lifetime figure and full story Smart owner unique_ptr = one duty; shared_ptr = shared lifetime; weak_ptr = observe, then lock() to try. Shared ownership does not synchronize the pointee. Exclusive ownership · Shared ownership · Weak observation Raw storage Allocation obtains bytes; construction starts an object; destruction ends its life; deallocation returns bytes. Placement construction does not allocate. Allocation versus construction · Placement/lifetime figure Board in one breath: source → object → borrow/owner → value transfer → RAII cleanup → safe external reclamation. At every arrow ask: who owns it, how long is it valid, and what ends use? The notes above target a single landscape page when rendered at ordinary study-note scale. The diagrams and answer keys below remain the linked detail, not required reading for every review pass. One story: from source text to responsibly released resource
Caption: Resource safety starts with the object model but ends only when the external-use contract permits release. A C++ destructor is not a GPU completion fence. Four figure briefs Use one row as a small revision card. Open its figure to see the caption and the surrounding worked example. The four cards supplement the existing notes and ownership boards. Card Short note Figure and explanation Check yourself Build Declare to compile a call; supply the definition to link it. Header guards act inside one translation unit. CPP-01 · two build lanes Why can a call compile yet fail at link time? Borrow Reallocation can dangle a path; slot assignment can keep it live while changing the entity. Validate, then reacquire. CPP-02 · lifetime versus identity Can the same address still reach the wrong entity? Move Construction creates a destination; a move operation may transfer duty. The source remains alive under its type’s contract. CPP-03 · two live objects, one duty Why does std::move(x) alone release nothing? GPU release RAII triggers the selected cleanup protocol; GPU completion governs when native release is safe. CPP-04 · deferred reclamation Which owner keeps the device and pending release queue alive? Answers: translation sees a usable declaration but linking still needs the definition; yes, semantic invalidation can preserve a live slot; std::move changes expression category and requires a consuming operation; the renderer must explicitly own the queue/device until all pending duties complete. Ownership decision board
Caption: Pick semantics first, syntax second. A raw pointer usually borrows; it does not extend lifetime. Shared ownership is a relationship, not a generic safety upgrade. Need Recall Common trap Borrow briefly T&, T*, span Caller must preserve lifetime and validity. Own exclusively unique_ptr<T> get() borrows; release() transfers the duty. Own jointly shared_ptr<T> Control-block safety does not synchronize T. Observe jointly owned object weak_ptr<T>::lock() Check the returned owner; expired() then use is a race. Release a native handle Custom/domain deleter Match the API, device/context, and allocator. RAII: move cleanup from branches into scope
Caption: Partial construction is safe only for responsibilities already held by fully constructed members/guards. A naked raw handle between acquire and adoption is a leak window. Storage, object and occupant are different states
Caption: Destroying an occupant does not necessarily free its storage. Same address does not mean same object. Correct alignment, size, construction, destruction and replacement rules still apply; std::launder does not construct or revive anything. The four questions to ask at a resource boundary Layer Ask Example Storage Which bytes, with what size/alignment? Arena slot large and aligned enough for Widget. Object Which live typed occupant? Widget has completed construction. Ownership Who ends its lifetime/releases the handle? Move-only GpuBuffer owner. External use When is reclamation safe? GPU completion fence/timeline. Retrieval prompts
Why can a stack object own heap or GPU resources? What does RAII automate, and what release timing must a GPU wrapper still know? Why is shared_ptr copying not a synchronization policy for the pointed-to object? Why does weak_ptr::lock() give a stronger test than checking expired() first? How can a weak_ptr keep control-block storage allocated after object destruction? What is the difference among new T, ::operator new, construct_at, destroy_at, and deallocation? Why does unique_ptr<Derived> converting to unique_ptr<Base> require a correct base destruction contract? What exactly does std::launder not do?
[!answer]- Compact key Scope-based owners run cleanup on normal exit and unwinding. External completion is a separate condition. Shared-pointer thread safety concerns ownership bookkeeping, not arbitrary pointee mutation. lock() atomically attempts to obtain a strong owner. Weak observers can keep the control block, but not the managed object’s lifetime, alive. A new-expression combines storage allocation and initialization; allocation functions alone only acquire storage; construction starts an object lifetime; destruction ends it; deallocation returns storage. Base deletion needs a valid virtual destructor or a deleter retaining the concrete type. launder can obtain a pointer to an already-live object only under its rules; it is no general repair tool. Teach the full ownership story · Part coverage · Dependency Map Added retrieval prompt Borrow: T& or const T&. Consume: unique_ptr<T> by value. Retain shared lifetime: shared_ptr<T> by value. Borrow an existing shared handle: const shared_ptr<T>& only for that call. Use a matching deleter for non-memory resources. Rebuild the API lab. Requests and replaceable backends — M011 retrieval experiment A renderer’s command is one of several known shapes; the runtime backend is one implementation of a common contract. These are two different decisions, so redraw the story without looking: command value → active alternative → borrowed submit call → virtual override → checked visitor → logical result → correctly destroyed owner. Then explain what remains separate from the story: the GPU’s completion and native-resource release rules. From memory, reconstruct the situation What the answer must account for Why can a union’s storage not be treated as several simultaneously live objects? One active member and the correct lifetime transitions; a byte pattern is not a type tag. How does a request prove its form? variant discriminant, checked get_if / visit, and possible exceptional valueless state. Why does a base reference call the derived implementation but a copied base value not preserve it? Static type, dynamic type, subobjects, virtual dispatch and slicing. Why is the interface destructor virtual? Destruction through an owning base pointer must reach the derived destructor; external GPU use has its own completion rule. What does a diamond with a virtual common base mean? Two inheritance paths reach one most-derived common-base subobject, not a mandated memory offset. What can each cast prove? static_cast follows a statically permitted conversion; dynamic_cast can runtime-check polymorphic relationships; reinterpret_cast does not create objects; const_cast does not legalize writing to genuinely const storage. Why must two handles with the same slot but different generations compare unequal? Identity includes the occupant generation; equality still does not prove current liveness. Why does the overridden reserve body see 2 through a base view but 7 through a derived view? Default argument from static type; virtual body from dynamic type. Can <=> always produce a total order? Integer ID fields can support strong ordering; NaN yields unordered floating comparisons and demands an explicit container key policy. Can we claim this is the fastest dispatch architecture? No: compare allocation, memory layout, branch behavior and optimizer effects on the same workload. Blank-file reconstruction: Recreate Clear, DrawMesh, Upload, Request, Backend and CountingBackend with a single exclusive owner; verify command counts, derived destructor execution, failed runtime cast, slicing, shared virtual base, generation-aware equality, NaN’s unordered comparison, overload selection and static default-argument binding. Full code and the checked build command are in the M011 C++20 laboratory; complete derivations and failure explanations are in the continuous narrative. Do not infer Kairo or GPU execution from this standalone test. One request, one transaction, callbacks that may outlive their caller — M012 reconstruction Read the complete M012 narrative only after attempting this recall route. The important picture begins with an editor requesting a resource and ends with either a fully published asset or the original published store unchanged.
The first thing to reconstruct is why each arrow is necessary. The request’s count must be distinct from an asset index, because identical raw integer types do not carry the same domain meaning. The file must be decoded as checked bytes, not by assuming any pointer cast creates a live WireHeader. Preparation must be private because callbacks or render systems must never observe half-constructed state. Every acquired handle must have one owner before a throwing operation can intervene. Publication needs a precise boundary: an exception before the commit must not modify existing records under the stated guarantee; a callback that throws afterward is a different event requiring its own policy. Reconstruction question Minimum evidence the reader must produce Why is a raw std::size_t a dangerous API for bytes? Show accidental unit mixing; write explicit ByteCount with explicit conversion back. Can a function pointer close over a local variable? No: a plain pointer carries a callable identity; extra state needs a context, whose lifetime is separately guaranteed. Why is a member-function pointer not an ordinary callback address? Explain the required instance and demonstrate object.*member invocation. What does a functor or lambda actually store? Draw state fields or references; contrast capture of an integer, pointer, view and this. How do value and reference captures differ after mutation? Predict snapshot 10 and live view 20; explain why a deferred reference may dangle. What changes when a lambda is stored in std::function? Type erasure, copyable target, possible storage cost, empty-call error; no guaranteed inline capacity. Which exceptions cause cleanup, and what cannot be rolled back? Distinguish stack unwinding/local RAII from preexisting external side effects. What are the basic, strong and no-throw guarantees? State valid-but-changed, unchanged observable state, and non-escaping exceptions; give each an example. Why must the native resource move be non-throwing? Trace vector growth, element relocation, and the relevant strong-guarantee conditions. Why can’t input validation live only in assert? NDEBUG can remove it; show typed invalid-input errors separately from programmer invariant failures. What do bit_cast and trivially copyable prove? A constrained representation-value operation, not a portable six-byte disk schema. Why is a typed pointer into an arbitrary file unsafe? Length, alignment, lifetime, alias rules, endian and padding are independent checks. How do we demonstrate rollback? Reproduce counts: (0,0,0), (1,1,0), (1,2,1), (2,3,1), then 0 live at destruction. Blank-file laboratory: Rebuild ByteCount; the fake device; the move-only Resource; the private AssetRecord; AssetStore::upload returning a typed result; function/member/functor callbacks; value/reference and owning-lifetime lambda captures; and a six-byte little-endian serializer. Compile under C++20 and warnings as errors, execute the deliberate failure after handle acquisition, then repeat under -DNDEBUG. The tested reference and exact commands are in the M012 lab and the source/evidence record. Do not classify this exercise as complete learner mastery until it can be reconstructed and explained independently. One asset pipeline, many types — M013 retrieval The preceding recall exercise ended with a safe, published asset. Now the editor wants the same preparation and publication guarantees for meshes, textures with different channel counts, and shader records. We must avoid duplicating stores without erasing type safety. Redraw this path from memory, then justify every boundary rather than reciting template vocabulary:
Imagine one Mesh containing three unsigned indices, one Texture<4> containing twelve texels, and one Texture<3> containing five texels. Explain why a trait gives 12, 48 and 15 source bytes, then derive why the checked batch accumulator returns 75. Show why a bound such as texel_count > max/Channels must be checked before multiplication. Finally explain why none of these counts establishes the actual GPU allocation size. Now reconstruct the implementation without opening the reference. Start with template<class T> function-template deduction. Build template<class T, size_t Capacity> with fixed optional slots and explain why the non-type capacity changes the class specialization. Provide the full AssetTraits<Mesh> specialization and the partial AssetTraits<Texture<Channels>> specialization, then contrast class-template specialization with function overloading. Derive U& & → U&, U& && → U&, U&& & → U&, and U&& && → U&&. Use those results to show why meshes.emplace(input) makes a copy while meshes.emplace(std::move(input)) selects a move path; do not assume the moved-from vector must be empty. The next reconstruction must connect a heterogeneous parameter pack to a checked fold. Show what happens for zero arguments and why a fold’s grouping is not itself a universal left-to-right side-effect guarantee. Then implement the earlier std::void_t SFINAE detection pattern and a clearer Uploadable concept with compound requirements. State exactly what a requires expression checks and what it does not execute. Constrain emplace with std::constructible_from and show why the overload route(const T&) selects the constrained path for supported assets and the generic fallback for UnknownAsset. Finally prove publication. If the published count is c, slots [0,c) are live and slots [c,Capacity) are empty. When the constructor throws in slot c, the count is not incremented. Reconstruct the deliberately failed CheckedShader(-1) attempt and show why the previously published version 3 remains valid and version 4 can use the next slot. Explain what would break if we supported deletion, stored raw references after the depot’s lifetime, invoked the API concurrently or replaced the CPU-only record with an asynchronously used GPU buffer without retirement bookkeeping. Evidence and full explanation: the M013 narrative, the tested C++20 laboratory and the 16-part coverage map. The test checks representative semantics, not the learner’s independent ability to reconstruct these decisions or current Kairo implementation details. The tile planner makes a choice — M014 reconstruction This recall path belongs after the full M014 narrative and the C++20 lab. Its purpose is to rebuild the decision chain from memory, not to duplicate an encyclopedia of template keywords. Picture one 8×2 RGBA texture tile, a budget of 64 bytes, a 64-byte CPU buffer, and a counting recorder. Before the renderer tries to use it, the planning layer must establish what is known from the type and what still depends on the incoming data. Draw this path, then explain each transition and its failure condition:
A correct reconstruction should derive (8\times2\times4=64) bytes from the uncompressed source representation, then explain why (8\times3\times4=96) fails the budget. It should show why a 4×4 RGBA request with no buffer fails only when the verification tag demands a real payload. The metadata-only 4×4 RGB path may report 48 planned bytes, but it has not proved any upload complete. Show how overflow is rejected by checking (x > \mathrm{max}/y) before multiplication, not by multiplying and inspecting the wrapped result. Rebuild PixelTraits<Format> using std::integral_constant and distinguish the fact that a type is empty from an assertion that it costs zero bytes in every containing object. Demonstrate an if constexpr RGBA branch and contrast it with a normal runtime if. Write a constexpr function that accepts either compile-time or runtime arguments; then change the problem so that a consteval function demands a valid compile-time tile definition. Explain why constinit permits a mutable, single-threaded diagnostic counter but does not make it const or atomic. Derive the four-bit Morton lookup without memorizing its answer. Spread (x=3) to binary 00000101 and (y=5) to 00010001. Shift the second pattern and OR the results to recover decimal 39. Construct the sixteen-entry table during constant evaluation. Then explain when a small lookup table might lose to shift/mask arithmetic because memory traffic and locality matter. From that setup, implement a stateless policy and a stateful budget policy with the same validate operation. Use TilePlanner<Format,Policy,Recorder> to compose the behavior without a runtime backend switch. Show why RecorderBase<Derived> may call Derived::record_impl only when it is genuinely part of an appropriately derived object; compare this static dispatch with a runtime-selected std::function target. Construct VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag and explain exactly how overload resolution chooses a validation path from the caller’s tag type. Finally compare normal empty-policy membership, private empty-base inheritance, and [[no_unique_address]] membership. On the tested Linux compilers their respective sizes were 16, 8 and 8 bytes; the rule is a permitted optimization, not a universal numeric contract, and compilers can treat the attribute differently. A complete blank-screen test recreates the accepted 64-byte RGBA plan, rejected 96-byte budget attempt, rejected empty verified payload, accepted 48-byte metadata-only RGB plan, and rejected overflowing extent. The recorder receives exactly two plans in the demonstrated sequence; failed requests do not reach it. Then state why this is not a real GPU resource, performance benchmark, atomic transaction for arbitrary throwing recorders, or proof of thread safety. The evidence ledger preserves the exact compiled commands and original fourteen-part mapping: M014 traceability · verification record. A growing asset store must preserve its promises — M015 retrieval A previously working fixed-capacity asset depot now grows, removes assets, accepts work in different scheduling orders, and lets the editor find items by name. Do not use the following as a replacement for the derivations in the complete M015 chapter. Start with this diagram and explain why its arrows and lifetime boundaries exist:
First distinguish size from capacity, and prove why reserve(2) creates zero live elements whereas resize(5) creates five. With a geometric capacity sequence 1,g,g²,..., derive the sum of relocation work and explain why an individual append can still have linear latency while amortized append cost remains constant. State the operations that invalidate vector pointers and the difference between an append with spare capacity, one requiring reallocation, a middle erase and reserve that does or does not change capacity. A pointer does not move itself when the vector relocates. Then reconstruct the identity protocol. Slot zero holds generation one; a handle {0,1} reaches it. After erase, that occupant is destroyed, its generation advances, and a new asset occupies slot zero at generation two. Draw why {0,1} no longer resolves. Explain what happens if generation wraps, if a raw Asset* or span was retained across reallocation, or if the renderer still has an asynchronous GPU read in flight. Distinguish a CPU identity check from the device-completion requirement. Show the two injected publication failures: one before any slot change, another after a new slot has been populated but before the name index becomes discoverable. Prove why the rollback resets the candidate and removes a newly appended unpublished slot; explain why the test’s successful outcome is not an unrestricted claim about arbitrary throwing user callbacks or all allocator behaviors. Now change the workload. A fixed-size channel array needs std::array, not vector growth. A front/back event stream makes deque attractive, but its iterator stability differs from that of its existing element references. A list can transfer a node with splice while keeping an iterator to an unaffected node; a forward_list needs the predecessor for erase_after. Explain what those guarantees cost in nodes, pointer chasing and cache locality compared with a contiguous vector scan. Next give two lookup problems. For ordered traversal and range queries, consider std::map / std::set, with logarithmic comparison-based behavior. For name-to-handle lookup or membership, use std::unordered_map / std::unordered_set and explain expected versus worst-case complexity. Write a hash that returns zero for every string; twenty-four distinct names now collide in the same bucket without becoming equal. Derive load_factor = size/bucket_count, explain what max_load_factor(0.5) and reserve(96) request, and state why rehash invalidates unordered iterators but does not generally invalidate references to surviving elements. Finally build the scheduling choices from user needs: a FIFO queue, LIFO stack, and a priority_queue whose comparator orders priority 3 before priority 1 and earlier sequence numbers before later ones within equal priority. Explain why priority_queue does not promise tie stability unless the comparator defines it. Finish by distinguishing borrow from ownership. A span<const uint8_t> carries a range while its byte vector remains alive and stable; it does not own the bytes. A string_view may point into only the middle of a stored string and need not be NUL-terminated at its end. Copy "stone" into std::string before destroying or modifying the source. Describe why the local observed short-string capacity of 15 cannot be advertised as a portable SSO specification. Actual reconstruction witness: M015 C++20 lab, compiled and run with GCC sanitizers, Clang, and a GCC release-style build. A learner should be able to recreate the sequence of checks without the reference and explain every failure. Original 20-part mapping · Exact test and provenance ledger. Do not claim personal mastery or real Kairo/GPU verification merely because this standalone model passes. Query the registry without confusing identity and a snapshot — M016 reconstruction The previous M015 exercise produced a generation-checked asset registry. The new problem is to report on assets without changing their live ownership and without assuming that a handle stays current forever. Read the full M016 narrative before testing recall; the questions below should be reconstructed as one processing story, not as twenty memorized API names.
Starting with the five records brick.mesh (48 bytes, priority 2), sky.tex (64, priority 3), ui.tex (16, priority 3), terrain.mesh (128, priority 1) and rock.mesh (48, priority 2), answer each part in coherent explanations:
Describe each result’s meaning. Why does optional<AssetHandle> mean “possibly absent” but fail to distinguish an empty query from a missing name? Build ExpectedLike<AssetHandle,LookupError> as a C++20 model. Explain exactly what its has_value() contract requires before value() is accessed and why it is not a full replacement for C++23 std::expected. Then distinguish that result from an Inspect/Upload/Evict variant and from a diagnostic any. Predict a wrong any_cast. Rebuild the report shape. Group count and error count in a pair and three report fields in a tuple. Show that auto [a,b] = pair copies this pair, while auto& [a,b] = pair aliases it. Explain why a named struct can be clearer at a long-lived public API boundary and why a borrowed structured binding needs an owner that outlives it. Prove the traversal capabilities before selecting the algorithm. Classify istream_iterator<int>, forward_list<int>::iterator, list<int>::iterator, deque<int>::iterator and vector<int>::iterator according to input, forward, bidirectional, random-access and contiguous iterator concepts. Why can std::sort operate on the vector’s random-access iterators but not directly on list iterators? Why may binary search over forward iterators have logarithmic comparison count but linear iterator advances? Choose ordering by what the editor needs. Write a comparator that first orders byte counts, then asset names so equal byte counts have deterministic tie breaking. Explain why std::sort need not preserve the order of comparator-equivalent records and why common introsort-like implementations are not mandated by the C++ standard. For descending priorities, write stable_sort and predict the relative order of sky.tex vs ui.tex and brick.mesh vs rock.mesh. State the strict-weak-ordering requirements the comparator must satisfy. Partition only when the task is binary membership. Use std::partition to put mesh records before non-mesh records; verify both halves and use partition_point on the resulting already-partitioned range. Explain why the two groups are not automatically sorted and why partitioning does not promise to retain original relative order. Say when stable_partition would be appropriate. Derive the binary-search boundaries. Once the byte-count ordering is [16,48,48,64,128], prove that lower_bound(48) returns index 1 and upper_bound(48) returns index 3. Explain why equal_range gives [1,3) and why lower_bound(50) points to index 3 despite having no match. Supply comparator overloads in both element/value and value/element orders. Describe why using a priority-sorted sequence here would violate the precondition. Compare one-off scanning with a maintained index. Use std::find to look for sky.tex in an unsorted name snapshot. Explain when this simple linear scan is preferable to building a fresh hash index, and when repeated lookups should instead use the registry’s already maintained name index. Transform and reduce with the correct numeric meaning. Derive [48,64,16,128,48] using std::transform and an output back inserter, then calculate 304 using an explicit std::size_t{0} initial accumulator. Write the ordered std::accumulate fold and explain why std::reduce may regroup operations, even if a particular run happens to use one thread. Use (10{20},1,-10{20},3) to derive both 3 and 4 from different floating-point groupings. State separate overflow, accuracy and deterministic-reproducibility policies. Erase at the correct ownership boundary. Starting with {1,2,3,4,5,6}, use remove_if to keep odd IDs but demonstrate that the vector still reports size six until erase destroys the suffix. Then use C++20 std::erase_if to remove the two texture records from an owned report snapshot, leaving three rows. Explain why the live asset registry has not evicted those assets and what additional generation validation, index cleanup and GPU retirement a real eviction would require.
Blank-file witness: reconstruct the program in asset_query_algorithm_lab.cpp with active failure checks, compile under C++20 with warnings as errors, then rerun with -DNDEBUG and sanitizers. The reference was actually run with GCC 14.2 ASan/UBSan, Clang 17 and GCC release flags. Reconstruct the expected values before running it; a passing executable is not a substitute for understanding the data/iterator/lifetime contracts. Audit: the original 20-part mapping and the source and verification ledger. The registry’s live concurrency, the separately named Kairo implementations and the learner’s independent reconstruction remain unverified here. From borrowed reports to module boundaries — M017 reconstruction The Phase 6 report used an owned snapshot so that sorting and erasing metadata did not mutate live engine state. The next problem is making that report composable without accidentally copying intermediates, choosing where its scratch allocations live, and sharing its API with separately compiled consumers. The full explanation is the M017 continuous chapter. Reconstruct the mechanism below from the problem, not by reciting the names of its twenty C++ features.
First reconstruct what the loop means. Draw the hidden range variable, begin iterator, end sentinel and increment/compare/dereference sequence behind a range-for. Define a cursor that holds a borrowed pointer to the snapshot vector and a numeric index, and makes operator++ skip retired slots. State the invariants for normal, end and default-created iterators; do not dereference the end. Explain why your cursor models std::forward_iterator and why it does not model random access or contiguity. With one 512-byte retired texture and live byte counts 48,64,16,128,48, predict exactly five visits and total 304. Next reconstruct laziness and lifetime. Compose views::all(rows) | views::filter(...) | views::transform(...) to obtain four names from those live rows with at least 48 bytes. Explain why merely forming the pipeline does not copy all four names into a vector and why iterating it later can call the predicate again. Predict why it is wrong to rely on a precise predicate invocation count for arbitrary repeat traversals. Compare views::all(lvalue_vector) with views::all(rvalue_vector) and explain how a ref_view can satisfy borrowed_range without keeping the vector itself alive. Conversely, explain why an owning view storing the vector need not qualify as a borrowed range when the view’s own destruction destroys the data. Use a projection only when the search needs one property. Without constructing a separate names vector, use std::ranges::find(rows, "sky.tex", &Row::name) and predict the record’s byte count. Sort an owned copy by &Row::bytes and state why the 512-byte retired row will still appear at the end unless you filtered it first. Discuss why the source vector’s contiguity does not make a filter view a writable random-access container. Compare AtLeastBytes{48} against an equivalent threshold-capturing lambda, giving a plan for benchmarking actual instruction and allocation costs instead of asserting one form is always faster. Now choose who owns allocation. Build a typed TrackingAllocator<T> that shares statistics across copies and rebindings, uses proper alignment and pairs successful storage acquisitions with deallocation. Explain why allocation is not the same as constructing a T object, and why allocator equality/propagation matter when a container moves or swaps. Then replace the compile-time allocator type with a std::pmr::vector and a std::pmr::unordered_map, both pointing to a counting memory_resource. Explain how unordered buckets/nodes and nested PMR strings may require allocator propagation, and why the resource must outlive both containers. Derive the arena lifetime, not just its common-case speed. Give a 128-byte aligned scratch buffer to a monotonic resource, then allocate 2,048 64-bit values. Explain why the initial buffer cannot contain the entire request; the resource must obtain upstream blocks. Predict why destroying the vector does not immediately free those blocks and why destroying/releasing the arena later can. Repeat with a 64-byte buffer and null_memory_resource upstream and predict std::bad_alloc. State the difference between a frame scratch lifetime and staging memory still held by an asynchronous GPU operation; neither the presence of PMR nor a move-only vector resolves the missing completion fence. Finally build an actual module graph. In separate files, put a :rules partition containing an exported 1,024-byte preview budget, a primary export module allmight.asset_query interface that re-exports that partition, and a module allmight.asset_query; implementation unit defining make_preview. Compile in dependency order. Write two separate importing translation units that use an exported inline function, link them with the implementation, and explain which declarations are exported and why that is distinct from C++ namespace naming or C language linkage. Build asset_query_interop.hpp as a header unit before using import "asset_query_interop.hpp";; compare this with an ordinary #include and explain macro/toolchain implications. Then expose a small versioned C header declaring int allmight_asset_approved_v1(uint64_t); build a C11 consumer using gcc and link it with the C++ wrapper and module objects. Explain exactly what this test establishes about the chosen GCC14 toolchain, and why it does not certify ABI stability across unrelated compilers or plugin versions. The real sources are the tested C++20 CPU lab and the executable module graph script. The local runtime lab passed GCC14 ASan/UBSan, Clang17 and GCC14 release; the module graph passed GCC14’s ordered module/header-unit build with three linked consumers. The original twenty-title coverage map and verification ledger distinguish that evidence from external Kairo audits and unmeasured performance. Personal mastery is earned only after independent explanation, tests and failure-case reconstruction; the authored lesson and one passing lab cannot grant it automatically. Preserve an asset while the engine changes — M018 reconstruction The editor selected a teapot before the asset service started deleting, reallocating and reusing storage. The renderer has independently compiled clients, several classes of resource handles and mathematical values from different coordinate frames. Reconstruct the API by starting with the event, not with a memorized list of PIMPL, concepts and expression templates. The complete reasoning lives in the M018 continuous chapter. The actually compiled service and its test program are in the test laboratory and the multi-TU build. Reconstruction 1 — identity, storage, and ABI. A mesh occupies slot zero in catalog A at generation one, and the client retains a handle. The vector reallocates, the mesh is erased, and a second mesh occupies the same slot. Explain precisely why a pointer might become invalid on reallocation, why a stale index could identify the wrong mesh, why a generation alone does not distinguish two separate catalogs, and why a MeshTag prevents a texture handle being silently passed to a mesh operation. The correct handle is a value containing a type-level kind and catalog/slot/generation runtime identity. A valid lookup compares all required fields and checks that the slot still holds a live value. After erase, the old generation must fail even when the slot is reused. The returned optional MeshInfo is a copy, so keeping it after erase cannot dangle, although its description is now stale. Confirm with the executable’s delete/reuse and cross-catalog tests. Reconstruction 2 — the public header is not the implementation. Write a declaration of an asset service that contains only an incomplete Impl and a unique pointer to that implementation. Explain why the destructor and move assignment must be defined where Impl is complete. Identify which client recompilations PIMPL can avoid and which ABI questions remain. Then identify the actual costs: one implementation allocation in the constructed design, pointer indirection and possible out-of-line call overhead. PIMPL is appropriate for a relatively cold service boundary, not automatically for every inner-loop vector, task or splat. Name the deep-const hazard: an owning pointer stored in a const public object does not in itself make the pointee immutable. Reconstruction 3 — three floats are not automatically the same mathematical value. Demonstrate why a world-space displacement and a camera-space displacement must be different C++ types, while also explaining the actual linear or affine transform that converts between them. Show why a point requires translation but a direction does not, why a normal may require inverse-transpose transformation, and why a quantity in meters cannot simply be added to a quantity in seconds. The phantom marker constrains type checking without adding a stored tag field; the underlying numeric representation does not perform a coordinate transform. Compare a fixed-size Vector<float,3,WorldSpace> with a runtime span requiring an explicit extent check. Explain why the supplied RealScalar concept intentionally rejects integers and user-defined autodiff scalars. Reconstruction 4 — materialization is both a performance and a lifetime decision. Trace eager a+b+c. Then trace a SumExpr storing references and evaluating operator[](i) on demand. Construct the dangerous saved outer expression that refers to a destroyed temporary inner node, and explain why its later evaluation is undefined behavior. Rewrite the example so the inner expression outlives evaluation. Explain how aliasing, SIMD, floating-point reassociation and compiler optimization affect the claim that lazy evaluation must be faster. The tested vectors produce (12,15,18); matching output is necessary but cannot alone establish absence of hidden allocations or the safety of every expression tree. Reconstruction 5 — own storage or embed links? Compare an intrusive task stack, where the task contains its next pointer and must outlive its membership, against a forward_list owning its elements. Show what breaks when a linked Task is destroyed, moved or inserted twice. The tested stack rejects duplicate membership and unlinks on pop. That is not a safe general-purpose ownership scheme for arbitrary user destruction. Predict how allocation, locality and mutation patterns could make either representation preferable. Reconstruction 6 — interrogate the machine rather than assuming zero cost. Compile the assembly probe with optimized GCC and Clang. Find the named externally visible function. Decide whether the templated addition was inlined and whether there are calls or unnecessary transfers on that compiler/target. Explain why a different ISA, link-time optimization, compiler flags or fast-math setting can produce different machine code and numerical results. State a fair baseline and define actual comparable workloads before declaring one catalog representation faster. A successful presence check for an assembly symbol is a build witness, not a timing benchmark. Final synthesis. Draw the lifetime sequence from editor selection to catalog erase and eventual GPU retirement. Distinguish three independently necessary guarantees: the CPU logical handle remains validated, the public C++ representation remains insulated as promised, and a GPU resource stays alive while submitted work may still read it. The M018 sample tests the first two in a limited CPU setting and does not implement the third. Compile under release -DNDEBUG and explain why the test program uses throwing checks instead of ordinary asserts. Then independently implement an asset handle with one additional version or session policy, state its invariants and design negative tests that could falsify those invariants. Mastery criterion: without looking up the code, reconstruct the public header, its out-of-line implementation, the validation predicate, an exception-safe reuse transition, a typed fixed/dynamic math interface, a lifetime-safe lazy expression evaluation, and a falsifiable compiler-cost experiment. Reading the answers is not evidence of independent reconstruction. Make the rejected operation part of the lesson
Read the figure: type checks decide whether the operation has the right meaning; lifetime checks decide whether its borrowed objects still exist. Both must hold. A successful type check does not extend an operand’s lifetime. Prompt Short answer Full explanation Two vector types differ; is mixing prevented? Test the actual eager, lazy and materialization operations. Every path needs the same scalar/space/extent restrictions. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#The delayed path must preserve the same mathematical contract Does a named inner expression become constexpr? Naming extends this node’s usable lifetime; it does not make references to automatic locals valid in that constexpr initializer. The saved lab uses const. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Expression templates: delaying evaluation can remove an intermediate and create a lifetime bug Why forbid copying this intrusive stack? Two head pointers can share hooks; popping one clears membership while the other still points at that node. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Intrusive storage exposes a different ownership contract Who survives stack destruction? Caller-owned linked tasks must survive at stable addresses; the destructor clears hooks without deleting tasks. [[tools/m018/m018_lab.cpp Reconstruct: predict the sequence A.push(task), copy A to B, B.pop(), A.push(task). Explain the duplicate-pop failure in the unchecked design and why the current stack rejects copying before execution. Then draw task/stack destruction order and show a valid unlink-and-reuse sequence. GPU interfaces and cooperation — shortest useful recall Column 1: Prompt Column 2: Recall answer Column 3: Expand immediately Size, alignment, stride? Recall answer Payload extent, legal start addresses, distance between elements. A 12-byte vec3 can require 16-byte start alignment. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract Is a texture-table index ownership? Recall answer No. Keep its referenced generation and allocation alive through pending uses. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership Workgroup versus subgroup? Recall answer Workgroups cooperate with shared storage and barriers; subgroups expose a smaller execution collective. Width is not universally 32. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock What does scan allocate? Recall answer Nonoverlapping output ranges: counts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> become offsets <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions Atomic, ordering, barrier? Recall answer Protect an operation; govern visibility/order; rendezvous with specified memory effects. These are different contracts. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions Can out-of-range lanes return before a required group barrier? Recall answer Generally no. Supply neutral values while preserving the barrier participation contract. Expand immediately [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions Explain the two barriers in tiled matrix multiplication: one protects complete tile loading; one protects reuse after every consumer finishes. Explain why a later dispatch still needs the API’s execution and memory dependency, rather than assuming a dispatch boundary flushes everything. API resource stages A name, initialized API object, allocated storage, initialized bytes and completed use are different states. glCreateBuffers establishes the object; a storage command establishes capacity; null initial data does not mean zero-filled bytes. Open the worked API distinction. A nonzero integer alone proves neither a safe draw range nor safe retirement. Temporary objects — retrieve the lifetime boundary Prompt Short answer Full commented witness Does every reference extend a temporary’s lifetime? No. The binding context matters; a borrowed view never owns its source. [[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Turn the lifetime rule into a scope trace. Open 02 - C++ - Objects, Ownership and Lifetime - Visual Recall in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Destruction and partial construction — Destruction and partial construction Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism The destructor body precedes reverse member/base cleanup. Ordinary constructor failure destroys completed subobjects but not the incomplete whole; failure after a delegating target completed has a distinct cleanup case. RAII binds resource release to an owning object’s lifetime. M010 extends the cleanup invariant to files, locks and native handles, and distinguishes destruction from external resource completion. A destructor can enqueue deferred release when an asynchronous user still holds the resource. Constructor failure remains safe when each acquired duty is immediately represented by a completed owner member. Prerequisites
Member order and delegating constructors — Reverse cleanup depends on the order and completeness of subobject construction. Storage duration and object lifetime — Cleanup belongs to an occupant’s lifetime, not merely a numeric storage address.
Used by
Assignment and exception guarantees Move operations and moved-from states RAII and resource handles
Recall and next depth Reconstruct both recorded failure event arrays. Pending: smart owners, polymorphic cleanup and explicit lifetime restart. Written coverage does not demonstrate personal mastery. Source and navigation Teaching mechanism and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map. Open Destruction and partial construction in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Sources and Code Anchors — Sources and Code Anchors Phase 8 - Source analysis and verification Seven user-supplied excerpts are lesson material, not independent instructions. Their merged numbered headings cover every Part 701–800. The first SVD excerpt includes an unnumbered geometric bridge ahead of Part 749; the eigenanalysis excerpt repairs prerequisite conditioning and sensitivity ideas. Both were integrated in the proper story locations. P8-A through P8-G are provenance labels only:
P8-A, Parts 749–769 and the SVD geometric bridge: /Users/swayamsingal/.codex/attachments/414e0258-cdcc-4ca8-9175-08d1583061df/Pasted text.txt. P8-B, Parts 737–748 and the conditioning/eigenanalysis repair: /Users/swayamsingal/.codex/attachments/835165b7-2308-43dc-b2b7-063a6f1b7049/Pasted text.txt. P8-C, Parts 701–711: /Users/swayamsingal/.codex/attachments/a87acda7-eaab-41ac-a080-836be6fd3f4f/Pasted text.txt. P8-D, Parts 712–721: /Users/swayamsingal/.codex/attachments/3557029e-4039-48eb-b6a5-043ac6213268/Pasted text.txt. Fixed conversion rejects non-finite input before rounding/casting. The supplied range checks alone do not reject NaN. Fixed multiplication/division use proved int64 intermediates and checked destination narrowing. Negative nearest-even rescaling uses unsigned magnitudes and quotient/remainder; it never negates INT64_MIN or adds a potentially overflowing positive half-scale. C++23 signed shifting is not described as universally undefined. Instead the lab uses scaled multiplication and an explicit rounding algorithm to avoid confusing modular shift behavior, floor, truncation and desired rescaling. The source’s lrint quantizer follows the active rounding direction. The teaching quantizer declares nearest-even, validates finite samples/scales, and bounds the ratio before integer conversion. It is not represented as identical production behavior. Offset code q+8 is distinguished from two’s-complement INT4. Half-step quantization bounds exclude clipping and finite-parameter/evaluation error. Smaller groups trade adaptation for metadata, without a universal monotonic quality guarantee. Full-group asymptotic bits/sample are distinguished from exact ceiling-based storage for small/partial groups. Binary16 loss scaling is not presented as a cure for already-large values; BF16 keeps exponent width but not every FP32 endpoint or precision property. BF16/half NaNs are explicitly canonicalized in the toy converters; raw tensor words preserve bits without signaling-NaN arithmetic. Parser bounds use subtraction after offset validation; shape products are checked before multiplication; exact length and a 4096-element resource cap precede allocation. Zero-copy mapping requires representation, bounds, alignment, lifetime and permitted typed-access rules—not merely an offset divisible by four. The dump helper rejects zero/excessive row width, advances by remaining bounded length and uses a local formatting stream. Error metrics promote float operands before subtracting when evaluated in double. Scalar reconstruction error is not task-level accuracy. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Floating-point addition and absorption — Floating-point addition and absorption Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism Addition aligns significands to a common exponent before adding/subtracting and rounding. At 2^24, upward binary32 spacing is 2, so adding 1 is a tie absorbed to the same even endpoint. 1.5+0.15625 aligns by three bits and gives 1.65625 exactly. Prerequisites
Significand and hidden bit — Significant digit positions determine alignment and what leading digits cancel. Exponent bias — Effective exponents must be decoded before comparing scale and shifting. Guard round and sticky bits — Aligned-away information must survive sufficiently to choose the correct rounded neighbor.
Used by
Floating-point reassociation — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid. Pending: A full software adder must handle classes, signs, range and every rounding mode; current trace is not that implementation. Source and navigation M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map. Open Floating-point addition and absorption in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Alignment and padding — Alignment and padding Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Alignment A restricts valid object starts to addresses divisible by A. alignof reports type alignment, which need not equal sizeof; alignas requests a supported stronger alignment. Padding fills layout holes and rounds array stride. Under 1/4/1 member rules, byte–uint32–byte uses offsets 0/4/8 and size 12. Power-of-two masks test low bits; checked align-up avoids unsigned overflow. Prerequisites
Byte and octet — Byte units define both storage offsets and significance digits. Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity.
Used by
Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts — Phase 6 uses this established foundation in its geometry narrative. ABI and object layout — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Internal and tail padding — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Packed structures and misaligned access — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. Dynamic allocation and heap — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites. SIMD and GPU data layouts — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.
Recall and next depth Derive 12 bytes from six payload bytes and safely align 0x1003 to eight. Pending: Over-aligned allocation, GPU layout rules and instruction-specific costs. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map. Open Alignment and padding in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Significand and hidden bit — Significand and hidden bit Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004 Definition and mechanism The significand supplies significant digits; the exponent supplies scale. A normal binary value begins 1.f, so its leading one is implied, not stored. Binary32 fraction F contributes F/2^23; subnormals instead begin 0.f. Prerequisites
Binary32 — The concrete fields provide the representation used in this mechanism. Positional notation — Negative powers of two give fractional digits their exact weights.
Used by
Floating-point addition and absorption — Significant digit positions determine alignment and what leading digits cancel. Cancellation and loss of significance — Significant digit positions determine alignment and what leading digits cancel. Floating-point encoding and decoding — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Subnormals and gradual underflow — uses this mechanism in its explanation. Machine epsilon — uses this mechanism in its explanation.
Recall and next depth Reconstruct the concrete example in the definition and identify its validity assumptions. Pending: Explain why 23 fraction bits give 24 normal bits but not 24-bit relative precision arbitrarily close to zero. Source and navigation M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map. Open Significand and hidden bit in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Cancellation and loss of significance — Cancellation and loss of significance Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism Nearly equal magnitudes subtract to a small difference, amplifying prior operand errors by roughly (|a|+|b|)/|a−b|. Stored subtraction can itself be exact. The source binary pair 1753/1024 and 1751/1024 differs by exactly 2^-9. Prerequisites
Absolute and relative error — Discrepancy, magnitude and reference units define sensitivity and threshold significance. Significand and hidden bit — Significant digit positions determine alignment and what leading digits cancel. Conditioning and singularity — Input sensitivity is distinct from errors an implementation introduces.
Used by
Sterbenz lemma — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract. Stable reformulation — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract. Dot and cross-product rounding — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Bitwise OR — Bitwise OR Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001 Definition and mechanism Sets selected lanes while preserving lanes paired with 0; it cannot clear an existing 1. Per lane: only 0|0 is 0; the other three cases are 1. 0xAD | 0x40 = 0xED sets locked. Repeating the operation leaves the same result: OR is idempotent. It cannot clear an existing 1, so replacing a field requires a clear step. Prerequisites
Boolean algebra — The logical domain is false/true.
Used by
Bit packing — uses bitwise or as part of its representation or reasoning. Logical versus bitwise operators — uses bitwise or as part of its representation or reasoning. Carry-lookahead and parallel-prefix adders — uses bitwise or as part of its representation or reasoning.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Shift-and-add multiplication — Shift-and-add multiplication Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002 Definition and mechanism Each set multiplier bit selects a shifted multiplicand partial product; an exact product of two <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit values may need <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </math> bits. Multiplier bit i selects multiplicand shifted i positions. 13×11 uses 11=1011₂, hence 13+26+104=143. Keep the shifting multiplicand in the widened type; shifting a uint16_t variable repeatedly discards high partial-product bits even if the accumulator is uint32_t. Prerequisites
Shift operations — Logical right shift fills high positions with zero; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit. Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.
Used by Connect later chunks here when they use this concept. Recall and next depth Explain shift-and-add multiplication without the label, work the example above, then state the assumption whose removal would change the result. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Allocator fragmentation — Allocator fragmentation Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, e.g. 37 bytes requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11. External fragmentation is free space split into holes incapable of satisfying one contiguous request, e.g. three separated 20-byte holes cannot supply one 60-byte block. Metadata overhead is an additional cost. Prerequisites
Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.
Used by
Huge pages and TLB reach — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
Recall and next depth Distinguish slack, metadata, and separated holes. Pending: Coalescing, size classes, virtual commitment and measured overhead. Source and navigation C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth Fragmentation is wasted allocation capacity caused by request shapes and allocator policy. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block because of alignment, size classes or rounding. External fragmentation is free memory split into pieces that cannot satisfy a larger request even when total free bytes are sufficient. A game or graphics workload amplifies the issue because lifetimes are structured: per-frame temporaries, long-lived assets, streaming resources and transient staging data behave differently. Using one general heap for all of them can mix lifetimes and make reuse less predictable. A useful experiment records requested bytes, committed bytes, peak live bytes, largest free span, allocation count and reuse over time. Frame arenas eliminate external fragmentation inside a frame by resetting wholesale; pools trade generality for fixed-size reuse; free lists require split and coalesce policy. Fragmentation is not measured by the process uses a lot of memory alone. Residency, allocator metadata, page commitment and application-owned slack must be separated before choosing a remedy.. Open Allocator fragmentation in Volume 1

Backward error measures how much the input must change for the computed output to be exact. Stability concerns algorithm errors; conditioning concerns problem sensitivity. Small backward error can coexist with large forward error. Prerequisites
Absolute and relative error — Discrepancy, magnitude and reference units define sensitivity and threshold significance. Conditioning and singularity — Input sensitivity is distinct from errors an implementation introduces.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Object construction and storage reuse — Object construction and storage reuse Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism Initialization creates an occupant whereas assignment replaces an existing occupant’s state. Ordinary constructor failure and post-target delegation failure have different complete-object cleanup behavior. Storage needs sufficient size/alignment before object initialization can complete and start an ordinary lifetime. construct_at and destroy_at separate object life from backing storage. A cast alone does not construct arbitrary types. Some specified operations implicitly create implicit-lifetime objects; replacement and launder have additional preconditions. M010 adds the resource-management view: placement construction or construct_at uses already-provided storage; it does not allocate that storage. destroy_at ends the occupant’s lifetime, while an arena separately decides when to reuse or release its bytes. Explicit destruction is safe only inside a protocol that prevents accidental second destruction. See Placement construction and explicit lifetime management. Prerequisites
Storage duration and object lifetime — Backing-storage duration must be distinguished from the occupant’s start, destruction and replacement.
Used by
Object identity and generation handles — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract. Return values and copy elision Constructors and invariant establishment Relocation versus move Placement construction and explicit lifetime management
Recall and next depth Give an example, explain why the rule exists, and identify which guarantee would be missing if the prerequisite were ignored. Pending: explicit lifetime restart, smart ownership and allocator protocols. Source and navigation C009 development C007 teaching chapter · Source coverage · Dependency Map. Direct local binding can extend lifetime, but a returned parameter reference cannot transitively extend it. Aggregate braces and parentheses differ for reference members; new-initializer extension does not last as long as the allocated holder. Prerequisites
Reference binding and converted temporaries — The chosen original or converted referent determines the destruction deadline. Storage duration and object lifetime — The referent and its backing storage must survive each alias use.

A checked borrow compares its saved epoch to the live pool counter before using the cached element. The pool counter must outlive the borrow; counters alone do not supply ownership, synchronization, race freedom or wrap immunity. Prerequisites
Borrow invalidation and logical identity — Invalidating mutations define the deadlines a saved epoch or deferred borrow must respect.

A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member. Width two at offset four owns positions 4–5 and values 0–3. The schema must fit the carrier and either forbid overlaps or explain their meaning. Prerequisites
Bit mask — A mask is a selection pattern, not an operation. Shift operations — Logical right shift fills high positions with zero; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit.
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Relocation versus move — Relocation versus move Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C009 Definition and mechanism A move leaves the source object alive; relocation ends its source lifetime as part of transfer. Move-construction plus old-object destruction is a relocation pattern, not general permission to memmove nontrivial objects. Proposal/toolchain facilities are not assumed portable in C++23. Prerequisites
Move operations and moved-from states — Traits, failure policy and relocation must distinguish source survival from source destruction. Object construction and storage reuse — A new destination requires a valid lifetime, independently of available bytes.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Null pointers and optional access — Null pointers and optional access Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism A null pointer designates no object/function; nullptr_t converts to appropriate null pointer values without choosing an integer overload. A non-null pointer is not a lifetime or bounds proof. Deleting a typed null object pointer is valid, but bare delete nullptr is ill-formed. Prerequisites
Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Storage relationships, bounds and lifetime distinguish valid access from a non-null value.
Used by Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created. Recall and next depth Explain absence, stale access and one-past access separately. Pending: optional/reference wrapper APIs and owning-pointer policies. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery. Source and navigation Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map Absence must be part of the type or contract A null pointer represents “no object at this address-bearing interface”; dereferencing it is invalid. That makes raw pointer nullability an API question. If a parameter must always designate an object, a reference or explicitly non-null wrapper communicates more than a nullable pointer plus a comment. Optional ownership and optional observation are different. A std::unique_ptr<T> may be empty while also owning when nonempty; T* may be nullable but usually says nothing about ownership; std::optional<T> stores an optional value without indirection. Choosing among them should follow lifetime and absence semantics rather than syntax convenience. Null checks also do not prove lifetime. A non-null dangling pointer is still invalid, and a pointer can become logically stale even if its numeric address is later reused for a different object. Tests for optional APIs should cover absent state, present state, transitions between them, moved-from ownership and invalid external identifiers. Avoid sentinel pointer values other than the language-defined null representation unless a low-level ABI explicitly owns that convention.. Open Null pointers and optional access in Volume 1

Scope locates a name’s binding; lookup resolves a spelling to declarations. A local x can hide ::x without destroying it. A block-scope static has a local name but persistent storage. Qualified lookup names a namespace or class explicitly. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: UNORM and SNORM — UNORM and SNORM Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism UNORM decodes q/(2^n-1); UNORM8 code128 gives128/255. SNORM commonly clamps q/(2^(n-1)-1) at -1, so -128 and -127 both map to -1 for eight bits. Prerequisites
Affine quantization and zero point — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Used by Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism. Recall and next depth Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it. Pending: Hardware/API conversion and supported format use must be verified per target; sRGB is separate. Source and navigation Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map Reconstruction depth An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>-bit UNORM integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> represents a real value approximately in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>q</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math> Quantization reverses that map with a declared rounding rule and saturation. The endpoint denominator matters: dividing by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> </math> would make the largest code fail to represent exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>. This is why a normalized color channel can round-trip its endpoints even though most interior values incur quantization error. SNORM maps a signed integer code to approximately <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. APIs differ in how the most-negative integer is treated, so the format specification—not intuition—owns the exact decode rule. This matters for normals and tangent vectors: decoding produces components, not a guaranteed unit vector. A sampled normal map usually requires later reconstruction or normalization and a coordinate-space convention. A useful test suite checks endpoint codes, monotonicity, round-trip error bounds, saturation outside the nominal domain, and the API’s exact most-negative SNORM behavior. Treating UNORM/SNORM as small floats hides where nonlinear color encoding, signed-vector normalization, and integer filtering contracts actually enter.. Open UNORM and SNORM in Volume 1

Generate Gᵢ=Aᵢ AND Bᵢ creates carry locally; propagate Pᵢ=Aᵢ XOR Bᵢ passes carry through. Expanding Cᵢ₊₁=Gᵢ OR (Pᵢ AND Cᵢ) permits parallel carry computation. Detailed prefix networks and wiring trade-offs remain future work. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Weak observation and ownership cycles — Weak observation and ownership cycles Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism std::weak_ptr<T> observes a shared_ptr ownership group without increasing its strong count. lock() atomically attempts to create a temporary strong owner; the result is empty if the managed object is no longer alive. Replacing one edge of an otherwise all-strong ownership cycle with a weak observation can allow the strong count to reach zero. A check with expired() followed later by access is not equivalent to a successful lock(). enable_shared_from_this joins the already-established shared ownership group; it must not create a second shared_ptr control block from this. Little endian emits the low octet first; big endian emits the high octet first. The 32-bit value 0x12345678 becomes 78/56/34/12 or 12/34/56/78 respectively. It does not specify intra-byte bit order. Explicit unsigned shifts/masks define an external representation independent of native host order. Prerequisites
Byte and octet — Byte units define both storage offsets and significance digits. Bit significance — Distinguish byte significance from where it is stored.

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Unit roundoff — Unit roundoff Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C005 Definition and mechanism Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions. Repeated-rounding bounds use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>γ</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mo><</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, under the stated rounding and range assumptions. Summation error also depends on operand magnitudes; this is not a universal relative-error guarantee. Prerequisites
ULP and representable spacing — Adjacent representable points define rounding candidates, errors and step distances. Rounding to nearest ties to even — Midpoint parity determines discarded-tail decisions and the normal relative-error bound.

Modulo m retains the remainder class after division by m. An unsigned N-bit domain uses m=2ᴺ: 250+10 becomes 4 when stored in eight bits, and 0−1 becomes 255. Narrow operands may promote first, so identify the operation type separately from the destination type. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Integrity and authenticity — Integrity and authenticity Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message. Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash. A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> and compute a tag such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mi>K</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash. A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available. HMAC construction For hash block size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> </math>, normalize key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> to one block, then compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mi>K</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>o</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math> The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message. tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector. Key management is part of authenticity A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:
the key is embedded publicly in the executable; keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation; a compromised key is never rotated; comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment; replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.
Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols. Production boundary The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code. Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.. Open Integrity and authenticity in Volume 1

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Foundations Bible — Volume I: From Bits to Computation, C++, Memory and Systems: Fixed-width integer types — Fixed-width integer types Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism Native bool is not a portable wire/GPU field; validate an explicit zero/one encoding. Floating type names do not guarantee exact IEEE formats; is_iec559 alone does not identify binary32. int need not be32 bits; sizeof(char)==1 measures a C++ byte and CHAR_BIT is at least8. Plain char is distinct from signed/unsigned char and its signedness is implementation-defined. size_t represents object sizes, not a stable serialized field. Query numeric_limits for digits, lowest, max and floating capabilities. A container’s size_type is not universally required to be exactly size_t. <cstdint> exact-width types express binary layout contracts; least and fast families have different portability goals. When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Exact-width typedefs are optional on implementations lacking suitable types. size_t represents object sizes and ptrdiff_t differences. Prerequisites
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent. Byte and octet — An octet is exactly eight bits.
Used by
